checks.claim: Key: green plants make their own food from water and air (carbon dioxide) with the energy of sunlight; the process is photosynthesis
checks.note: Grokipedia: plants 'use light energy'; inputs are 'light energy (typically from sunlight), CO2 absorbed from the atmosphere, and H2O'; outputs 'carbohydrates such as glucose ... and O2'.

checks.claim: Wrong: Pollination (carrying pollen from flower to flower), not food-making
checks.note: 'the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma of the same or another flower'. Context's 'from flower to flower' is a fair simplification (self-pollination aside). Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Germination (a seed sprouting)
checks.note: 'the process by which a dormant seed, spore, or other reproductive structure resumes growth'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Transpiration (water leaving the leaves as vapour)
checks.note: 'the evaporation of water from the aerial parts of plants', mainly through stomata in the leaves. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Key: carbon dioxide is the gas from the air a plant uses to make its food
checks.note: Inputs: light, 'CO2 absorbed from the atmosphere', and water. Also https://beyondpenguins.ehe.osu.edu/?p=2290: 'plants convert carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen'.

checks.claim: Wrong: Oxygen (plants take in oxygen, but for respiration, not for making food)
checks.note: Ohio State: 'Respiration ... is the breaking down of sugars (and oxygen) to provide energy'. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, not an input. Context states this correctly. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Nitrogen (most of the air; not part of the sugar)
checks.note: Dry air is 'nitrogen (N2) ... 78.08% by volume'. Glucose is C6H12O6 (no nitrogen). Legumes' root bacteria fix N2, but for protein, not for food-making by photosynthesis. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Carbon monoxide (a poisonous gas from burning fuel)
checks.note: 'colorless, odorless, tasteless' gas 'arising chiefly from the incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels'; toxic through its 'high affinity for hemoglobin'. Not a photosynthesis input. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Scene: a candle burns out in a closed jar; a sprig of mint is put in; after some days a candle burns in it again (Priestley's 1771 experiment, told without his name)
checks.note: Priestley's own words: 'on the 17th of August 1771, I put a sprig of mint into a quantity of air, in which a candle had burned out, and found that, on the 27th of the same month, another candle burned perfectly well in it'. Ten days, so 'several days' is fair. Grokipedia Photosynthesis tells the same: 'After several days of exposure to sunlight, the air regained its purity'.

checks.claim: Detail: the jar 'stands in sunlight'
checks.note: Priestley's own account does not mention light (Ingenhousz in 1779 showed light was needed: 'the process ceased in darkness or shade'). Because the stem tells a generic scene and names no one, adding sunlight makes the scene scientifically correct, not a misreport. No fix needed.

checks.claim: Key: the mint gives off oxygen in sunlight, which lets the flame burn
checks.note: Outputs include 'O2 released into the atmosphere'. Fire needs oxygen: https://grokipedia.com/page/Fire_triangle ('All three elements must be present simultaneously').

checks.claim: Wrong: Carbon dioxide (and context: it smothers a flame)
checks.note: 'Carbon dioxide (CO2) extinguishers displace oxygen'. In light the mint takes CO2 in, net. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Nitrogen
checks.note: Nitrogen is the inert bulk of air; a plant does not release it, and it does not feed a flame. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Water vapour
checks.note: The mint does give off water vapour (transpiration), but water vapour does not let a flame burn; the stem asks which gas lets the flame burn. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the same oxygen from plants is what people and animals breathe
checks.note: Oxygenic photosynthesis 'represents the primary source of free oxygen'. (Algae and cyanobacteria also contribute; 'plants' is a fair T1 simplification.)

checks.claim: Key: the leaves make the food in the first place (sugar made in the leaves, carried to the tuber)
checks.note: Leaf is 'the primary photosynthetic organ of vascular plants'; potato stem tubers 'store starch but derive initial reserves from leaf translocation'. Grokipedia Tuber: starch 'synthesized from photosynthetic products translocated via the phloem', energy from 'aboveground photosynthesis'. Sucrose import from leaves confirmed in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/pmid/20137087.

checks.claim: Wrong: Its potatoes (the tuber does assemble the starch: is the choice partly true?)
checks.note: The tuber itself turns imported sucrose into starch (sucrose synthase, then AGPase), so 'the potato makes its starch' is true in a narrow sense. But the stem asks which part makes the food 'in the first place', and the tuber makes nothing from light: an underground tuber cannot photosynthesize (it greens only if exposed to light, per https://grokipedia.com/page/Potato). The qualifier excludes it; the context also explains the sugar-to-starch step. Defensible as wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Its roots
checks.note: Roots are underground and not green; they take up water and minerals, not make food (https://beyondpenguins.ehe.osu.edu/?p=2290: plants take up 'water and minerals from soil, but not food'). Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Its flowers
checks.note: Potato flowers are 'typically white to purple', not the food-making green parts; their small green sepals contribute negligibly. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: sugar travels down to the potatoes and is stored as starch; food is made only where light reaches green parts
checks.note: Starch 'accumulates as grains ... in amyloplasts (long-term in tubers, seeds)'; Ingenhousz: only green parts released the gas, and 'the process ceased in darkness or shade'. Tuber is an underground stem (Grokipedia Tuber), so 'potatoes sit in the dark soil' is fine.

checks.claim: Key: chlorophyll is the green substance that catches sunlight for making food
checks.note: 'primary photoreceptor for capturing sunlight during photosynthesis'; a green pigment; name from Greek chloros, green, and phyllon, leaf.

checks.claim: Stem: in autumn the chlorophyll breaks down and the yellow and orange that were there all along show through
checks.note: Shortening days 'halt chlorophyll production'; 'enzymatic degradation of existing chlorophyll molecules'; reveals 'pre-existing carotenoids', yellows and oranges 'inherent to the leaf throughout the season', in deciduous trees. (Reds are newly made anthocyanins; the stem does not mention red, so no issue.)

checks.claim: Wrong: Carotene
checks.note: Carotenoids do help harvest light in the antenna complexes, so 'catches sunlight' is partly true of carotene; but the stem asks for the GREEN substance and itself names the yellow/orange ones as different. Carotene is orange. Truly wrong in the stem's terms.

checks.claim: Wrong: Starch
checks.note: Starch is the stored food (grains in chloroplasts and amyloplasts), not a green light-catching pigment. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Nectar
checks.note: Sugary liquid made in flowers to draw pollinators; not green, not in leaves. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: carotene is one of the yellow-orange substances hidden under the green all summer
checks.note: Names beta-carotene and xanthophylls (lutein) as the main pre-existing carotenoids.

checks.claim: Key: the leaf makes sugar from water and carbon dioxide using light
checks.note: Outputs 'carbohydrates such as glucose for energy storage'; equation 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Sugar is right at T1.

checks.claim: Wrong: Protein (needs nitrogen, which water and CO2 lack)
checks.note: Leaves do build proteins, but not from water and CO2: 'Nitrogen is a critical component of amino acids, proteins', taken from soil (or via legume bacteria). H2O and CO2 hold no nitrogen. The stem's 'joins water and carbon dioxide' rules it out. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Minerals
checks.note: Mineral nutrients are 'absorbed primarily from the soil in ionic forms', not made by the leaf. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Salt
checks.note: Salts are minerals from soil water; a leaf does not make them, and neither water nor CO2 holds sodium or chlorine. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: sugar feeds the plant and can be stored as starch
checks.note: Glucose, sucrose and starch are 'broken down via respiration for ATP'; starch grains are the store.

checks.claim: Key: most of a tree's matter comes from air (carbon dioxide) and water
checks.note: NGSS 5-LS1-1 clarification: 'plant matter comes mostly from air and water, not from the soil'. Grokipedia Plant_nutrition: C, H and O come 'primarily from atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O), rather than soil minerals', about 89-96% of dry weight. Dry wood is about 50% carbon, 6% hydrogen, 44% oxygen (USDA FPL, https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/42245.pdf).

checks.claim: Wrong: From soil and minerals
checks.note: Van Helmont's willow: 5 lb shoot in 200 lb of dried soil grew to '169 pounds and 3 ounces' in five years while the soil lost 'only about 2 ounces'. Minerals are a few percent of dry mass. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: From sunlight and warmth
checks.note: Sunlight gives energy, not matter (NGSS PS3.D: energy captured by plants 'in the chemical process that forms plant matter (from air and water)'). Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: From dead leaves and twigs
checks.note: Plants take up mineral ions from the soil solution, not decayed matter as building material; litter decomposes into minerals (some organic N reaches roots via mycorrhizal fungi, a negligible share of mass). Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: an acorn grows into an oak
checks.note: 'the fruit of oak trees in the genus Quercus, consisting of a single seed', which develops into new seedlings.

checks.claim: Key: the grass caught its energy from sunlight
checks.note: 5-PS3-1: 'energy in animals' food (used for body repair, growth, and motion and to maintain body warmth) was once energy from the sun'; PS3.D: 'captured by plants in the chemical process that forms plant matter (from air and water)'. Matches the stem's 'walk about and keep warm'.

checks.claim: Wrong: drew it up from the soil
checks.note: Listed misconception: 'Plants get their energy from the soil through roots'. Soil gives water and minerals, not food energy. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: soaked it up from the rain
checks.note: Water is a raw material (H2O), not an energy source; light supplies the energy. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: took it in from the air
checks.note: The air supplies CO2 as a material; photosynthesis is 'converting solar energy into chemical energy'. CO2 carries no usable food energy. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: a cow spends hours every day eating grass
checks.note: 'total daily grazing time typically ranging from 6 to 9 hours'; cattle graze grasses, forbs and browse.

checks.claim: Key: photo (Greek phos, phot-) means light
checks.note: Wiktionary: photo- from Ancient Greek phot-, from phos, 'light'. (Coined 1893 by C. R. Barnes per Wikipedia Photosynthesis.)

checks.claim: Stem: synthesis means putting together
checks.note: Greek sunthesis, from sun 'with, together' and tithemi 'put, place'.

checks.claim: Wrong: Picture
checks.note: English 'photo' as a clipping of photograph means picture, but the stem asks what the old Greek word means; Greek phos is light. Truly wrong, and a good lure.

checks.claim: Wrong: Leaf; Wrong: Green (context: the Greek roots of chlorophyll)
checks.note: Chlorophyll is 'from Greek chloros for green and phyllon for leaf'. Neither is the meaning of photo. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: a photograph is named for the same word, as a drawing made with light
checks.note: Coined 1839 by John Herschel from phos, 'light', and graphe, 'drawing' or 'writing': 'drawing with light'.

unit_notes: All nine questions check out. Watch-points examined: (1) Potato: 'Its potatoes' is narrowly true for the final sucrose-to-starch step, but 'in the first place' makes the leaves the only defensible answer; keep the qualifier if the stem is ever edited. (2) Candle-and-mint jar: matches Priestley's 17 to 27 August 1771 trial (ten days); Priestley did not record sunlight, but the stem names no one, so the sunlit scene is correct science rather than a misreported history. (3) Mass from air and water: NGSS wording, Grokipedia Plant_nutrition, USDA wood composition and van Helmont's willow (169 lb 3 oz from 200 lb soil losing about 2 oz) all agree. (4) Carotene does help catch light as an accessory pigment, but the stem asks for the green substance, so it stays wrong.
